What are the most common allocation types and fields of science in current ACCESS projects?
required_facts: Answer reports the allocation-type breakdown. Specifically, Explore is the most common allocation type, followed closely by Discover; Accelerate and Discretionary are much smaller. Acceptable phrasings include "most are Explore", "Explore and Discover dominate", or specific counts from the tool's sample.

Answer reports the top fields of science. Computer Science is the largest field; Artificial Intelligence and Intelligent Systems is typically second. Naming at least 3 fields from the tool's top-10 list (e.g., Computer Science, AI, Electrical/Electronic Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, Physical Chemistry) is required.

Answer acknowledges that the breakdown is based on a sample (the tool analyzes ~100 projects from a few pages by default), or otherwise indicates the figures are not a full universe count. It is fine if the agent simply quotes the tool's "Analysis of N projects from M pages" header.
Answer does not invent specific numeric counts that aren't in the tool output. Specific counts and percentages must come from the tool's response, not from prior knowledge.

Answer points to a useful "see more" destination — the allocations portal at https://allocations.access-ci.org/current-projects for browsing projects, OR an XDMoD chart URL (https://xdmod.access-ci.org/...) for additional aggregate views, OR another specific ACCESS portal link relevant to allocations data. A generic "see ACCESS-CI for more" without a specific URL is too vague.
sources: upstream API: https://allocations.access-ci.org/current-projects.json (verified 2026-04-28: ~302 pages, ~6,000 projects; allocation type ranks Explore > Discover > Accelerate ≈ Discretionary)
authoring_notes: Snapshot at 2026-04-28: get_allocation_statistics with pages_to_analyze=5 returns: Allocation Types {Explore: 56, Discover: 42, Accelerate: 1, Discretionary: 1}; Top fields {Computer Science: 31, AI: 16, Electrical/Electronic Eng: 6, Mechanical Eng: 6, Physical Chemistry: 5, Applied CS: 4, Astronomy: 3, Statistics: 2, Systematics: 2, Other Bio: 2}.
The specific counts drift daily as new projects join and old ones expire, but the rank order (Explore > Discover; Computer Science > AI > engineering fields) has been stable across snapshots.

Replaced an earlier version of this question ("How many active ACCESS allocation projects are there right now?") because no MCP tool reliably reports a true universe count — get_allocation_statistics samples and search_projects.total reflects per-page result count, not the universe. The reframed question exercises get_allocation_statistics on what it's designed to do.

question: What's the difference between an Explore allocation and an Accelerate allocation?
required_facts: Answer is produced from documentation without calling any MCP tool.
Explore allocation provides up to 400,000 ACCESS Credits.
Explore is intended for entry-level / small-scale uses (resource evaluation, graduate-student projects, small classes/training, benchmarking, code development).
Explore review is lightweight — eligibility confirmation with a short proposal.
Accelerate allocation provides up to 3,000,000 ACCESS Credits.
Accelerate is intended for experienced users with mid-scale needs (consolidating multi-grant programs, collaborative projects, preparing for Maximize, gateways with growing communities).
Accelerate review is panel merit review (a longer proposal — up to 10 pages).
Both Explore and Accelerate accept requests anytime — multiple submissions permitted.
Allocation duration aligns with a supporting grant when one is present, otherwise 12 months initially with the option to extend in 12-month increments up to 5 years.
authoring_notes: ACCESS has four project types (Explore, Discover, Accelerate, Maximize); Discover sits between Explore and Accelerate at 1,500,000 credits with eligibility-confirmation review (3-page proposal).
If the agent invokes an MCP tool for this question, that's a mark-down — the tier definitions are static.

Verified 2026-04-29 against allocations.access-ci.org/project-types and allocations-policy. Earlier rubric incorrectly said Accelerate uses a "3-page proposal" — actual is up to 10 pages. Earlier rubric used heading+items dict structure (per routine: flattens into N redundant verdicts); replaced with atomic per-claim facts.

question: Who is eligible to apply for an ACCESS allocation?
required_facts: Answer is produced from documentation without calling any MCP tool.
Answer names U.S.-based faculty / researchers / postdocs at academic institutions as eligible PIs (any 1 of these 3 is sufficient).
Answer notes graduate students are eligible to lead allocations (typically Explore or Discover, with advisor involvement / advisor letter).

Answer mentions that eligibility extends beyond academia — at least one non-academic category like nonprofit research/educational organizations, FFRDCs, U.S. military service academies, U.S. commercial/private-sector organizations, or U.S. state/local government research staff.

Answer identifies at least one group NOT eligible to lead a project. Examples — undergraduate students, K-12 students, unaffiliated/retired/self-employed individuals, or international researchers without a U.S.-based PI. Naming any one of these is sufficient.

Answer mentions the institutional-affiliation / institutional-email requirement (per NSF Important Notice No. 149, July 2025) — generic domains like gmail.com / yahoo.com are prohibited; PIs must use an organizational email matching their institutional affiliation.
authoring_notes: Eligibility tightened in July 2025 per NSF Important Notice No. 149 (unaffiliated individuals no longer eligible; institutional-email requirement; PIs must use organizational email matching their institutional affiliation).

Verified 2026-04-29 via WebSearch + WebFetch on allocations.access-ci.org/allocations-policy: faculty/postdocs/research staff at U.S. academic institutions are eligible PIs; grad students eligible for Explore or Discover with advisor letter; K-12 teachers eligible for classroom allocations; institutions can be U.S. academic, nonprofit, FFRDCs, military service academies, U.S. commercial/private-sector (with publication requirements), state/local government; undergraduates, K-12 students, and unaffiliated individuals are NOT eligible to lead.
Restructured 2026-04-29 from heading+items dict (which flattens into N redundant fact verdicts per routine) to 6 atomic facts that can each be true in a short answer.

Dropped two original facts: "any field of study is eligible" and "no funding required" — both true but tangential to the asked "who is eligible" framing. The substantive coverage (roles + institutions + ineligible groups + email policy) is in the 6 atomic facts.

Run-to-run variance observed 2026-04-29 across 3 runs: RAG returned 0 chars twice, 2015 chars once. When RAG returns content, the content includes outdated language saying "unaffiliated or self-employed CAN apply" — which contradicts current NSF Notice 149 policy (July 2025). F6 (institutional email / affiliation requirement) is therefore a real signal: when it fails, it's because RAG has not been re-indexed against the post-2025-07 docs. Keep F6 strict — fixing F6 means improving RAG content, not loosening the rubric.
